The Treaty of Nanking. Signed on August 29, 1842, aboard a British warship in Nanking, or Nanjing as it's now spelled. It ended the First Opium War between Britain and China. The treaty forced China to cede Hong Kong to Britain, open five treaty ports to foreign trade, pay a massive indemnity, and grant Britain most-favoured-nation status. It marked the beginning of the Unequal Treaties era, in which Western powers extracted concessions from a weakening China. For once the dominant empire, China was humiliated and accelerated into decline.

The First Opium War was fought from 1840 to 1842. It started because China tried to halt British opium smuggling into the country. Britain invaded to force markets open. The Qing dynasty, militarily outmatched by British naval and industrial superiority, capitulated after losing major cities. The message was stark: Western military technology was superior to what China could muster.

Hong Kong was ceded to Britain in perpetuity. It would become Britain's gateway to China and later a global financial centre. China was forced to recognise Britain's sovereignty over an Asian territory. This was unprecedented. For centuries, China had viewed itself as the centre of the world. This humiliation for the imperial power was profound.

Five treaty ports were forced open to British trade—Guangzhou, Amoy, Fuzhou, Ningpo, and Shanghai. These cities ended China's monopoly over foreign commerce. China was forced to pay an indemnity of twenty-one million silver dollars. This was crippling for the imperial treasury. Britain was granted most-favoured-nation status, which meant any benefits granted to other powers would automatically be extended to Britain.

Trade restrictions on opium were removed. British merchants flooded China with opium, destroying millions of Chinese lives. Addiction became epidemic. Opium became one of the instruments of Western domination over China.

British subjects in China were exempt from Chinese law. This principle of extraterritoriality extended to other Western powers through later treaties. No Chinese representative signed the treaty. It was imposed unilaterally, establishing what became known as the Unequal Treaties template. China was forced to treat Britain as an equal power, reversing the Qing system of tributary relations where China stood at the centre.

The Treaty of Nanking is a watershed in Chinese and world history. It marks the moment China ceased to be the world's dominant power and became an object of Western exploitation. For the Qing dynasty, it was catastrophic. It revealed military obsolescence—Chinese junks against British steel ships and artillery. It revealed economic vulnerability and loss of sovereignty. For Britain and the West, the treaty vindicated the use of force to pry open markets. The Opium Wars demonstrated that industrial military technology could overcome continental empires.

The treaty spawned a century of similar treaties, French, American, German, and Russian, all extracting concessions from a weakening Qing. The humiliation burned deep in Chinese nationalist consciousness. It became a rallying cry for revolution—the Boxers, Sun Yat-sen, the communists. The treaty thus not only partitioned China among Western powers but also seeded the ideological currents that would eventually expel them. Hong Kong's cession, finally reversed in 1997, symbolises China's century of subjugation and its twenty-first-century resurgence.
